author: harness:claude-code

patch.value: A deleted item's id is immediately re-mintable, so one immutable history stream can hold two unrelated items and every integrity check still reports verified

An item id is not a permanent name. When an item is deleted, pm removes the item file and deliberately retains the immutable history stream, but the id-minting probe only asks whether an item FILE exists for a candidate id. Nothing consults the retained history stream, so any id whose item was deleted is immediately available to be minted again, and the new item's create entry is appended to the dead item's existing chain.

Proved deterministically in an isolated sandbox on 2026.7.28 using the reproducible-execution primitives shipped by pm-rbcvt2, which make the minted id a function of the seed:

  run 1, seed fixed-seed-alpha -> creates pm-yanz "FIRST original item", one comment added
  pm delete pm-yanz            -> item file removed, history/pm-yanz.jsonl retained with 3 entries
  run 2, SAME seed             -> mints pm-yanz again, creates "SECOND unrelated item"
  history/pm-yanz.jsonl        -> 4 entries: create, comment_add, delete, create

Two unrelated items now share one immutable stream, and every integrity surface reports success:

  pm history pm-yanz --verify --strict-exit -> ok true, entries 4, current_matches_latest true, exit 0
  pm validate --check-storage-integrity --check-history-drift -> ok true, no warnings
  pm health --summary -> ok true

Point-in-time reconstruction then answers two different questions with the same id and reports full confidence in both:

  pm get pm-yanz --at 2 -> title "FIRST original item", reconstructed true
  pm get pm-yanz --at 4 -> title "SECOND unrelated item", reconstructed true

The restore-any-version promise is therefore conditional on something nothing checks. A caller asking for version 2 of pm-yanz receives a different item's state, correctly replayed, with no signal that the id changed subject between version 3 and version 4. A second create entry in a stream is the discriminating symptom and no reader treats it as one.

Seeding made the collision deterministic but is not the cause. The hazard is structural and applies to ordinary random minting: with the default four-character base36 token the space is 1,679,616, the probe is blind to every deleted id, and the probability of recycling grows with both corpus size and delete volume. It also compounds across branches, where the probe cannot see the other branch at all.

This is distinct from its neighbours and must not be merged with them. pm-khdq (closed) covered the parallel-create TOCTOU where two live creates race for one id and the loser's FILE is overwritten; here there is no race and no file to overwrite. pm-qw1uw6 covers reconstruction CRASHING when a stream opens without a baseline entry; here reconstruction succeeds and returns the wrong subject. pm-nb4zwz covers disclosing a tombstone to a reader who asks for a deleted id; here the tombstone is not merely undisclosed, it is overwritable. pm-wlqxg3 is the universal replay gate and needs this defect fixed before its assertion is even well-formed, because "every version of every item" presumes a version belongs to exactly one item.

Minting a new id consults every durable record of prior use, including retained history streams for deleted items, so a previously used id is never reissued; A stream that would receive a second create entry is refused at write time with a structured error naming the prior use, rather than accepted and reported as verified; An existing stream containing more than one create entry is reported by pm validate as a data-integrity error with the id and the entry ordinals named, and by pm history --verify as a failed verification rather than ok true; Point-in-time reads across an identity discontinuity either refuse with a structured error or disclose the discontinuity as part of the result, so a caller can never silently receive another item's state; The check is available through the SDK identity primitives rather than only in the CLI, so MCP and other hosts inherit it; A regression fixture reproduces the recycling deterministically through a seeded reproducible execution and asserts the refusal, keeping the negative control permanently executable

message: File verified identity-recycling defect found by seeded reproducible execution

value.text: Second, concurrency-native path to the same terminal state (2026-08-02). Re-minting after delete is not the only way one history stream ends up holding two unrelated items: two branches that mint the same id independently produce exactly that, and the merge driver resolves the add/add as an ordinary field conflict — title, description and created_at go to the preferred side, the other item is annihilated into discarded_hash values in a receipt, and the merged stream carries two create entries. This item's first two acceptance criteria cannot prevent it, because across branches there is no shared durable record to consult at mint time; only the third criterion (a stream with more than one create entry is reported) covers the shared terminal state. Filed separately as pm-qx95lz because the cause, the prevention point (merge driver rather than mint probe) and the fix differ; the detector is the one thing the two share.
